entries.name: Limited discrepancy search
entries.definition: A backtracking tree-search strategy that repeatedly explores paths under an increasing upper limit on deviations from a successor-ordering heuristic; in the original binary formulation, taking the nonpreferred child consumes one discrepancy.
entries.identity_notes: The original LDS searches paths with at most k discrepancies in each pass. It differs from Korf’s improved LDS, which avoids revisiting leaves at the supplied maximum depth by allocating an exact discrepancy count there, and from depth-bounded discrepancy search, which bounds where deviations may occur. The original 1995 Figure 1 explores the nonpreferred child first when discrepancy budget remains; Korf’s 1996 presentation of original LDS uses the opposite within-pass order. The names do not establish identical visit sequences.
entries.mechanism: Run a depth-first probe with budget k, starting with k=0 and increasing through a sufficient maximum depth for a finite binary tree. When the budget is zero, follow the heuristic-preferred child. With positive budget, the original Figure 1 first probes the nonpreferred child with k−1 and then the preferred child with k. Return when a goal is found. Each pass permits at most k deviations, so earlier paths may be revisited in later passes.
entries.locator: Section 3 and Figure 1, printed p. 608 / PDF p. 2; Section 5.5, printed p. 611 / PDF p. 5
limitations: Completeness applies to exhaustive passes on a finite tree with a sufficient discrepancy/depth limit and adequate resources. A fixed early-pass cutoff is not a decision procedure for unsolvability.
The first goal found is not generally a minimum-cost or shortest-path goal. Successor preference is a search-order heuristic, not an admissible cost bound.
The curated original mechanism is binary. Counting any alternate child as one discrepancy and assigning rank-based discrepancy costs are distinct multiway extensions requiring an explicit policy.
Repeated at-most-k passes revisit paths. The subsequent ILDS paper qualifies the original redundancy argument and supplies cases where discrepancy search has no advantage over ordinary DFS.
The original paper references an LDS-BBS appendix that is not present in the inspected seven-page download. The bounded-backtracking hybrid is not asserted as part of this record.

entries.name: Improved limited discrepancy search
entries.definition: Korf’s discrepancy-search variant that uses a supplied maximum search depth and remaining discrepancy count to generate each path to that depth in the pass corresponding to its exact number of nonpreferred choices, avoiding the original method’s repeated maximum-depth paths.
entries.identity_notes: ILDS is the 1996 improvement to LDS, not a generic label for any later discrepancy-search modification. Its exact-count guarantee concerns leaves at the specified maximum depth; shallower leaves and internal nodes can still be revisited. The supplied depth bound differs from a bound on the depths at which discrepancies are allowed.
entries.mechanism: For each budget k from zero through the supplied maximum depth, recursively track remaining depth D and discrepancies k. In the binary Figure 3, visit the preferred child when D>k, leaving k unchanged; visit the nonpreferred child when k>0, reducing k by one. Both moves reduce D by one. When D=k, only nonpreferred choices remain possible along a path that reaches the depth bound. The printed procedure visits the preferred branch before the nonpreferred branch when both are allowed.
entries.locator: Improved Limited Discrepancy Search and Figure 3, printed p. 287 / PDF p. 2; Interior Node Overhead of ILDS, printed p. 288 / PDF p. 3
limitations: A valid upper bound on maximum depth is an input. A loose bound or pruning that creates shallower leaves reduces the benefit because those leaves may be visited on several passes.
Visiting each maximum-depth leaf once does not mean visiting every internal node once; repeated prefixes remain.
The complete uniform-tree expansion analysis is conditional on that tree shape. It does not establish an unconditional wall-clock advantage on pruned trees or early-terminated searches.
The procedure’s discrepancy priority does not guarantee that the first goal is shortest or globally minimum-cost. No universal superiority over DFS is asserted.
The 1996 prose gives a depth-three original-LDS path count inconsistent with its own displayed counting formula and the original paper’s trace. No literal 19-path count is adopted.

entries.name: First-come, first-served beam decoding
entries.definition: The sequence beam-decoding procedure described by Kasai and colleagues that stores completed hypotheses separately from the continuing beam and stops when the accumulated number of completed hypotheses reaches the beam width, returning the highest-scoring stored completion.
entries.identity_notes: FCFS here names a sequence-decoding policy, not first-in-first-out queue scheduling. Completed sequences leave the active beam and remain in a separate set. This differs from the paper’s vanilla beam decoder, where finished and unfinished hypotheses compete for the same beam slots, and from score-prioritized per-length best-first beam search. The original policy is the patience-controlled family’s p=1 case.
entries.mechanism: At each sequence length, expand the continuing hypotheses and scan the candidate pool in decreasing score order. Move an encountered EOS-ending hypothesis into the persistent finished set; otherwise keep it in the next continuing beam, up to width k. Stop during this selection when k completed hypotheses have accumulated and return the best stored completion. The paper also imposes a maximum generation length.
entries.locator: Figure 1 with p=1, printed p. 77 / PDF p. 1; Section 2 and Figures 2–3, printed pp. 78–79 / PDF pp. 2–3
limitations: The count-based stopping rule can discard unfinished candidates and is not a global optimality certificate or a guarantee of equality to vanilla beam decoding.
The record identifies the paper’s specified procedure. Claims about particular library defaults are historical context, not assertions about current software versions.

The simplified pseudocode assumes that candidate selection and completion return are defined. Exhausted candidate pools, absence of any EOS completion, ties and maximum-length handling require explicit implementation policies.
The score and any length penalty affect candidate selection and comparison of completed outputs. A fixed beam width alone does not determine output quality.
The paper’s favorable comparisons are task/model dependent; no numerical benchmark gain or universal generation-quality claim is curated.

entries.name: Patience-controlled FCFS beam decoding
aliases: FCFS beam decoding with controlled patience
entries.definition: A generalization of first-come, first-served sequence beam decoding that retains beam width k for continuing hypotheses but uses a positive patience factor p to stop when the accumulated completed-hypothesis count reaches at least k·p.
entries.identity_notes: This is the algorithmic stopping-policy variant introduced by Kasai and colleagues, not a standalone model, learned parameter or generic training patience rule. Setting p=1 recovers their FCFS baseline; changing p separates its finished-output threshold from its continuing-beam width.
entries.mechanism: Keep the FCFS candidate selection and separate persistent finished set, but replace the termination threshold k with k·p. Return the highest-scoring stored completion once that threshold is reached, subject to the method’s maximum-length limit. With integer completion counts, the displayed inequality corresponds mathematically to reaching ceil(k·p); this is an interpretation of the paper’s inequality, not a claim about rounding in any software library.
entries.locator: Figure 1 line 13, printed p. 77 / PDF p. 1; Patience Factor for FCFS, Section 2, printed p. 79 / PDF p. 3
limitations: The finite maximum length can end decoding before the completion threshold is reached. Empty finished sets and exhausted candidate pools need an implementation-specific outcome.
Increasing patience can expose more completions but does not guarantee better task quality, a globally optimal sequence, or equivalence to vanilla beam search.
The parameter is a stopping threshold, not a score upper bound or a proof that no unfinished hypothesis can improve the incumbent.
The source evaluates specific translation and news-summarization settings. English news summarization does not establish benefits for all languages, domains or tasks.
No current library default, runtime gain, numerical quality improvement or trained-model execution is claimed.

entries.name: Vanilla sequence beam decoding
entries.definition: A layer-based sequence beam decoder in which completed and unfinished hypotheses compete for the same k beam slots: finished hypotheses are carried forward unchanged, unfinished hypotheses are extended, and the top-scoring candidates form the next beam.
entries.identity_notes: This is the vanilla sequence-decoding policy contrasted with FCFS by Kasai and colleagues. It specializes generic breadth-first beam search by specifying EOS retention and competition for active slots. Finished outputs are not accumulated in a separate permanent set, and the procedure is not the score-prioritized per-length best-first decoder.
entries.mechanism: At each sequence length, construct a fresh candidate pool from carried-forward EOS-complete hypotheses and one-token extensions of unfinished beam members. Select up to k highest-scoring candidates for the next beam. The 2024 description stops when all retained hypotheses are complete, or at the maximum length. The 2020 standard-beam pseudocode explicitly resets the candidate pool at each layer and carries finished hypotheses unchanged.
entries.locator: Section 2 and Figures 2–3, printed pp. 78–79 / PDF pp. 2–3
limitations: A completed hypothesis can later fall off the beam because it competes with unfinished candidates. Its discovery alone does not reserve an output slot.
Finite beam pruning is not exact global MAP decoding. Different tie, length-score and maximum-length policies can change outputs.
At the length limit, an implementation must specify what to return if no retained hypothesis is EOS-complete; the simplified figures do not provide a universal failure policy.

Figure 2 in the 2024 paper omits initialization/reset of its temporary H pool. The fresh-per-layer interpretation is supported by the layer-based prose and the explicit reset in Meister et al. 2020 Algorithm 1; the record does not certify the 2024 figure as executable code.
The name identifies the source-defined policy, not a claim that all libraries or all uses of beam search implement it.
